title: Trump Election Dividend: How the $5,000 Payment Could Work and What You May Get
summary: President Trump has proposed a midterm election dividend for U.S. adults. This is how much he said Americans could get.
body_markdown:
President Donald Trump announced on Sept. 9 that every adult U.S. citizen would receive a $5,000 payment if Republicans keep control of both the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm elections.1 That could mean $10,000 for a married couple. At the moment, there is no approved check, rebate or[tax credit to claim](https://smartasset.com/taxes/tax-credits-2020) . The proposal remains a campaign pledge, and its implementation would likely require congressional action and funding. Here’s how the dividend might work, who may qualify and what your family could receive.


**While the proposed dividend remains uncertain, a**[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=trumpmidtermelectiondividend) **may be able to help you review your tax planning strategy and evaluate opportunities to manage your finances under existing tax laws.**


## Trump’s $5,000 Promise and What Needs to Happen First


Trump made the announcement at the Republican National Committee’s first midterm convention in Dallas, calling the payment the “Trump Dividend.”2 He compared it to a company paying out profits, saying it would be “very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders.”


Four days later, the president doubled down on his midterm dividend promise while speaking at the Amgen Irish Open. He said the country could “easily” afford the payments and added, “I always keep my pledge.”3


Neither appearance changed the basic hurdle: winning both chambers can’t put money in anyone’s account without a law to authorize and fund the payments.


Other presidents and candidates have tied cash to election results. On Jan. 4, 2021, the day before Georgia’s Senate runoffs, President-elect[Joe Biden](https://smartasset.com/taxes/biden-vs-trump-taxes) told voters in Atlanta that if they elected Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, “those $2,000 checks are going out the door,” referring to COVID-19 stimulus payments.4


After Democrats won both seats, House Ways and Means Chairman Richard Neal said the[American Rescue Plan](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/american-rescue-plan-biden-third-stimulus) ’s $1,400 pandemic checks, following December’s $600 payments, “finishes the job on the President’s promise to provide $2,000.”5


Campaign promises like these are generally legal. In Brown v. Hartlage (1982), the Supreme Court ruled that the First Amendment protects a candidate’s pledge to give voters a benefit when it would need normal government approval.6


The Election Law Blog called Trump’s pledge “almost certainly protected by the First Amendment against bribery or vote buying charges,” citing Brown v. Hartlage as the leading case.7


The Trump dividend would require congressional action to authorize and fund the payments.


## Who Could Qualify for the Trump Dividend


At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, the president promised to “issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.”


Pew Research Center estimates that approximately 250 million U.S. citizens age 18 and older are eligible to vote in the 2026 midterm elections.8 If all received $5,000, the total cost would reach roughly $1.25 trillion. However, the final number of recipients could be smaller if the administration establishes income limits or other eligibility restrictions.


The amount pledged to be paid out could be about $1.25 trillion (250 million × $5,000). For a comparison, that would be more than three times larger than the[third round of stimulus checks](https://smartasset.com/insights/coronavirus-third-stimulus-checks) passed in 2021, when the IRS issued over 175 million payments totaling more than $400 billion.9


Vice President JD Vance said[wealthy Americans](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/net-worth-states-2026) could be excluded, which would lower the total cost.10 The administration hasn’t shared details on that potential exclusion, so the actual cost can’t be estimated yet. Here’s what different households could receive based on the pledge as described:


### How Much a Household Could Receive From the Trump Dividend


Household Possible Payment Based on the Pledge What Is Still Unclear


Single adult citizen $5,000 Possible income limit


Married couple, both citizens $10,000 Whether higher earners would be excluded


Married couple with two children $10,000 based on the two adults Whether children could qualify


One citizen and one noncitizen spouse Potentially $5,000 Treatment of mixed-status households


**A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=trumpmidtermelectiondividend) can help you plan to use a salary bonus, tax refund or other windfall, whether you decide to pay down debt, build emergency savings or invest for future goals.**


Trump also said the dividend would have to be spent in the United States. However, the administration has not explained how such a restriction would be enforced or whether it would apply to particular purchases or transactions. Those details would need to be addressed if the proposal moves forward.


Despite the administration’s proposal, Americans largely remain skeptical. An Economist/YouGov poll found that only one-fifth of registered voters (21%) believe Trump will “definitely or probably” follow through on the pledge if Republicans keep control of Congress, while 57% said they don’t believe he will follow through on the campaign promise.11

## How the Trump Dividend Could Be Funded


The Constitution establishes that no money can be drawn from the Treasury without an appropriation made by law.12 That means Congress would have to authorize and fund the program before any payments could go out.


The Tax Foundation estimates that paying $5,000 to 250 million adults eligible to vote would cost about $1.25 trillion.13 The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) separately estimates that a $5,000 dividend would cost more than $1.2 trillion if paid in 2027.14


While Vice President JD Vance has said[tariff revenue](https://smartasset.com/taxes/is-it-possible-for-tariffs-to-replace-income-taxes) could help reduce the cost, the nonprofit projects that[new tariffs](https://smartasset.com/taxes/tariff-vs-tax) would raise roughly $1.4 trillion in net revenue from 2026 through 2035.15


If this estimate holds, one round of Trump dividend payments would use almost 90% ($1.25 trillion ÷ $1.4 trillion) of that 10-year projection. However, the Tax Foundation said that the federal government is already expected to run a deficit of nearly $1.9 trillion in fiscal year 2027.


> Moreover, the projected tariff revenue would be collected over 10 years and is already incorporated into federal budget projections, meaning it would not automatically provide additional funding for the dividend.


The CRFB calculates that adding a one-time dividend would push that deficit up to $3.1 trillion.


## How Trump Dividends Compare With Past Payments and Promises


Comparing past federal programs and proposed dividends could show which ones were approved, how they were funded and who received the money. Every direct payment in the table below that reached households had congressional funding behind it. The proposals that did not get funding were never paid.


### Timeline of Past Payments and Proposals


Year Payment or Proposal Amount Congress Funded It? Paid?


2008 Economic stimulus payment16 Up to $600 individual, $1,200 jointly, plus $300 per qualifying child Yes Yes


March 2020[CARES Act payment](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/coronavirus-stimulus-package) Up to $1,200 per adult Yes Yes


Dec. 2020[Second COVID payment](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/covid19-second-stimulus-checks) Up to $600 per adult Yes Yes


2021 American Rescue Plan payment Up to $1,400 per eligible person Yes Yes


2025 DOGE dividend proposal17 About $5,000 per taxpaying household proposed No No


2025 Tariff dividend proposal18 At least $2,000 per person proposed, excluding high earners No No


2025 Warrior Dividend19 $1,776 for qualifying service members Yes, through existing military housing funds Yes


A campaign pledge does not authorize a payment. For the Trump dividend, legislation passing both chambers and becoming law would matter more than the election result.


The proposed $5,000 per adult would exceed all three pandemic-era checks combined. An adult who received the full amount in each round got $3,200 ($1,200 + $600 + $1,400).


Taxes could also affect how much you keep. The 2021 stimulus checks weren’t taxable, and the Warrior Dividend was tax-free because it was paid as a military housing allowance. Congress has not created the Trump dividend, so its amount, eligibility rules and tax status have not yet been confirmed.


## Two More Midterm Election Payments You May Get


Separate from the proposed $5,000 Trump dividend, the administration has announced two other payments for eligible Americans. These include $500[Affordable Care Act](https://smartasset.com/retirement/medicare-vs-obamacare) refunds for nearly 1 million people in 30 states and a one-time $90[Medicare Part B](https://smartasset.com/retirement/medicare-part-b) premium rebate for approximately 20.8 million beneficiaries. Unlike the proposed dividend, these payments are not contingent on the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections.


The $500 refunds go to people in states who buy insurance through HealthCare.gov and receive no financial assistance toward their[monthly premiums](https://smartasset.com/insurance/how-to-deduct-health-insurance-premiums-if-youre-self-employed) . The White House said the money comes from excess fees collected to run the exchange.20


Federal health officials at the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services say 20.8 million people are eligible for the $90 rebate.21 Eligibility is limited to people living in the U.S. with Part B coverage under Original Medicare.


The rebate excludes people whose Part B costs are already[paid by Medicaid](https://smartasset.com/data-studies/medicaid-enrollment-2026) , higher earners who owe IRMAA and anyone enrolled in a private Medicare Advantage plan. Eligible beneficiaries are receiving the $90 rebate in October through direct deposit or a mailed Treasury check. The payment is intended to offset part of that month’s Medicare Part B premium.


## Bottom Line


Keep the proposed dividend out of your household budget until Congress approves funding and sets the eligibility rules and payment method. One qualifying adult might receive $5,000 and two might get $10,000, but neither amount is guaranteed. Continue covering bills and meeting savings goals with income you already have. Any payment that eventually arrives can then go toward overdue expenses, high-interest debt, emergency reserves or longer-term priorities.
